_comment: Guided tour for the PTO inspector. Steps point at real controls and wait for the user to press them. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: What a .pto is
steps.text:
One measurement, one file. The instrument file goes in byte-for-byte and is never decoded into a second copy beside itself; every result computed from it — bursts, decays, correlations, fits, selections — is written beside it, each carrying the operation and the settings that produced it.

This window only reads. Eight steps, about a minute; you press the buttons.

steps.title: Open a container
steps.text: Any .pto — browse for one, drag it onto this window, or pick it from the database. Dropping a vendor photon file (PTU, HT3, SPC) offers to pack it into a container first.

await.hint: Choose a .pto, by 📂 Browse or by dropping one on the window.

steps.title: What is in it
steps.text:
One row per object, in the order it was written. The columns are the container's own vocabulary: kind is what sort of thing this is, operation is what produced it (empty means it was carried rather than computed), and grain says what one row is.

Grain is the load-bearing one — nothing in a container is joined by position, so a dwell table and a burst table can live in the same file.

Click a row. Everything on the right follows the selection.

steps.title: How it got there
steps.text:
The provenance graph. Instrument file on the left, the last thing computed on the right, and every arrow a recorded derivation — not an inference from folder names.

Look for a node with two incoming arrows: a lifetime fit uses the bursts and the background. That is the case a tree view cannot draw without duplicating a node or dropping an edge, and it is why this is a graph.

steps.title: The numbers
steps.text:
A tabular payload opens in the shared table — sort, filter, hide columns, search, export. The headers carry the unit the column itself states, so a duration in milliseconds cannot be read as seconds.

A curve opens in Curve instead, with its axis units and scale taken from the stored columns: an FCS lag axis is milliseconds on a log scale and a decay axis is nanoseconds on a linear one.

steps.title: The settings are the identity
steps.text:
The details panel lists everything recorded — and the settings are not a label on the run: their hash is the run. Recomputing with the same settings rewrites that artifact in place; changing one produces a new artifact.

That is why nothing accumulates in a container and why no parameter ever has to be encoded in a file name.

steps.title: Open the tool that made it
steps.text:
A container records the operation, never the program — naming a ChiSurf plugin in the file would have made it unreadable by anything else.

So the index runs the other way: each tool declares which operations it performs, and this button opens the matching one on this same file. A double-click on a graph node does the same. A step no installed tool claims says so plainly.

steps.title: Before you delete the original
steps.text:
🔍 Verify re-hashes every payload and compares it against the checksum recorded beside it. Do this before deleting an original file: restorable without verification is only probably restorable.

The ? button beside this guide has the long version.
